decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker summarizes the overall goal without duplicate handling; client adds, “I also care about not ending up with the same link saved twice.”
decisions.note: At the initial specification gate, the client extends the presented goal with the reference duplicate-prevention requirement.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker’s goal summary omits set-aside handling; client adds that they need to “clear out or set aside things I'm done with without losing them by accident.”
decisions.note: At the initial specification gate, the client surfaces reversible set-aside behavior and its safety distinction.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker asks the client to paste a URL and select “Save bookmark”; client reports, “I saved that link.”
decisions.note: The prototype decision supports saving a bookmark by entering its URL.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker specifies fetched “title, description, site, icon, and original address” but no preview image; client calls it “exactly what I hoped for.” Rounds 5 and 11 continue to describe these details as complete without adding a preview image.
decisions.note: The presented metadata flow omits the reference-required preview image. The client approves without stating that difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker presents a readable card with title, description, site, icon, and address; client says it is readable and skimmable. Rounds 12–16 subsequently add visible tag pills.
decisions.note: Across the linked list-and-label presentations, cards expose the reference fields in a readability-first form.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker asks whether the checked save-and-show flow is complete; client responds, “When I come back later and click one of these saved cards, I'd expect it to take me straight to the original page.”
decisions.note: At prototype review, the client requests the missing original-URL navigation behavior.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker asks whether the existing flow is complete; client says they want to “tweak the title or description — both right after saving and later on.”
decisions.note: The client corrects the initially non-editable flow by requesting title and description editing.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker asks whether the flow is complete; client says an existing URL should “bring me back to the one I already have so I can edit that, rather than making a duplicate.”
decisions.note: At the save-flow gate, the client again supplies the missing reference behavior with its edit-existing outcome.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 maker presents clicking anywhere on a card to open the original page in a new tab; client confirms it “took me straight to the original article.”
decisions.note: The revised prototype conforms to original-URL navigation; using a new tab is an orthogonal UI choice.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 7–9 present editing the fetched title and description directly in the card after saving; in Round 9 the client confirms the changed title is saved and displayed.
decisions.note: The recorded post-save title/description editing decision conforms to that portion of the reference requirement.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 9 and 11 describe the settled flow as editing “immediately after saving” and making “in-card corrections now or later”; no pre-save editing is presented. The client approves the flow in Round 11.
decisions.note: The settled editor supports after-save editing but not the reference-required ability to edit auto-collected title/description before saving; the client does not surface that difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 client defers duplicate judgment until multiple links can be tested. Round 10 maker then presents a three-item library where re-saving an existing URL keeps the count at three, highlights the existing card, and opens its editor; client says, “That's exactly it.”
decisions.note: The Round 6 pending clarification is linked to its Round 10 disposition and counted once. The revised duplicate flow conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker declares the save-and-show flow complete with in-card corrections; the demonstrated editor covers title and description, and later labels, but no URL editing is presented. The client approves the complete flow.
decisions.note: The settled editing scope omits editing a bookmark’s URL. The client does not mention this reference difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker presents adding “typography” directly to a bookmark and retaining labels as visible pills; client says this is exactly how they picture organization.
decisions.note: The decision supports assigning multiple visible tags to bookmarks.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker presents manual label addition; client asks that an existing label “start suggesting itself as I type” so it can be selected rather than retyped.
decisions.note: At label-flow review, the client requests the missing existing-tag autocomplete behavior.

decisions.evidence: Round 13 maker presents labels as editable inside the bookmark editor as well as through quick-add; client asks to retain both paths.
decisions.note: Editing a bookmark’s tag assignments in the full editor conforms to the tags portion of REF-BM-04.

decisions.evidence: Round 14 maker presents typing “typo” and choosing the existing “typography” suggestion; client confirms the suggestion appears while typing and is selectable in one click.
decisions.note: The revised label entry behavior conforms to existing-tag autocomplete.

decisions.evidence: Round 15 maker asks whether creating, reusing, and displaying labels completes the flow; client adds, “I'd want to be able to take a label off a bookmark too.”
decisions.note: The client rejects completeness and requests the missing ability to remove a tag assignment.

decisions.evidence: Round 16 maker presents removing the “design” pill from only the current bookmark while keeping that tag available elsewhere; client confirms this is the desired behavior.
decisions.note: The revised tag-removal behavior correctly edits only the bookmark-tag relationship.

decisions.evidence: Round 17 maker scopes search to titles, descriptions, sites, URLs, and labels. Client states, “once I can jot my own little notes ... I'd expect those notes to be searchable.” Round 54 client repeats that notes should be searchable. Round 55 maker says private notes are deferred, and client explicitly accepts leaving them “for a later round.”
decisions.note: Linked specification and implementation-review sequence: the client explicitly states the missing note-search expectation and later accepts its deferral.

decisions.evidence: Round 54 client reminds the maker they want to “jot my own little private notes on a bookmark.” Round 55 maker states notes remain for a later cycle; client says, “I'm content to leave that for a later round” and wants it next cycle.
decisions.note: At implementation review, the client explicitly recognizes and accepts omission of bookmark notes. No markdown authoring/rendering is delivered in this cycle.

decisions.evidence: Round 18 maker confirms “capitalization-insensitive matching”; client responds that search should work “without caring about capitalization.”
decisions.note: The plain-search decision conforms to case-insensitive search.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 19–21 present selecting an exact label from either a card pill or label row and narrowing to only bookmarks carrying it; the client confirms both paths reach the same filtered view.
decisions.note: Both equivalent entry points conform to filtering by a specific tag.

decisions.evidence: Round 22 maker asks whether plain search plus label filtering completes finding; client refuses completion and requests “putting something in quotes so I get that phrase precisely.”
decisions.note: At the finding-flow gate, the client requests the missing quoted exact-phrase capability.

decisions.evidence: Round 22 maker asks whether finding is complete; client requests combining conditions such as “design links, but not the accessibility ones” and “this word or that word.”
decisions.note: The client surfaces missing Boolean inclusion, exclusion, and alternative matching semantics.

decisions.evidence: Round 22 client additionally requests “Mixing a typed word with a label ... links labeled ‘design’ that also mention ‘grid.’”
decisions.note: The client requests the missing reference rule that tag and full-text conditions can be combined conjunctively.

decisions.evidence: Round 23 maker presents the query “design patterns” in quotation marks returning only the exact phrase match; client confirms it means “those words in that order, and nothing looser.”
decisions.note: The revised exact-phrase behavior conforms.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 24 and 28 present tag terms as `label:design` and `-label:accessibility`; Round 29 declares finding complete with “typed shortcuts.” The reference `#tag` syntax is never presented. The client discusses the `label:` form as fiddly and approves visual controls but never states the missing `#tag` expectation.
decisions.note: The final search language does not support the specified `#tag` syntax, and the client does not surface that reference difference.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 24–29 present minus-prefixed label exclusion plus visible all/any controls, and then call finding complete. No AND/OR/NOT expression language, parenthesized groups, or quoted-literal operator rule is presented. The client approves the completed flow.
decisions.note: The controls reproduce some simple Boolean outcomes but omit the reference search-term grammar and grouping capability; the client does not identify those omissions.

decisions.evidence: Round 27 maker combines selected label “design” with typed word “grid” and returns only the bookmark satisfying both; client confirms it kept “both conditions at once.”
decisions.note: The demonstrated combination of tag and text conditions has the reference-required AND semantics.

decisions.evidence: Round 30 maker presents a labeled “Read later” control whose state and queue count change; client confirms the bookmark is clearly queued.
decisions.note: The decision conforms to marking a bookmark unread/read-later.

decisions.evidence: Round 32 maker presents a dedicated Read Later view containing only marked bookmarks; client calls it the dedicated unfinished-reading place expected.
decisions.note: The decision conforms to viewing unread bookmarks separately.

decisions.evidence: Round 34 maker presents selecting “In Read later” to remove the NASA bookmark from the queue while retaining it in All bookmarks; client confirms both outcomes.
decisions.note: The decision conforms to marking an item read and removing it from the unread list without deleting it.

decisions.evidence: Round 36 maker presents “Move to Archive,” removing the card from All Bookmarks and increasing the Archive count with restoration reassurance; client confirms this means set aside rather than lost.
decisions.note: The archive action conforms to reversible hiding from the default list.

decisions.evidence: Round 38 maker presents an Archive destination in side navigation containing set-aside bookmarks; client calls it “a view holding just my set-aside things.”
decisions.note: The decision conforms to a separate archived-bookmarks list.

decisions.evidence: Round 38 maker presents restoring an archived bookmark to All Bookmarks; client confirms it returned home and describes Archive as a safe holding place rather than a trash can.
decisions.note: Restoration establishes Archive as reversible and distinct from permanent deletion.

decisions.evidence: Round 38 client leaves ordinary-search exclusion pending. Round 39 maker then presents archiving an item from an active search, keeping it absent from All Bookmarks search while making it searchable inside Archive; client says this settles the lingering concern.
decisions.note: The pending archive-search expectation is linked to its Round 39 disposition and counted once; the behavior conforms to archive scoping.

decisions.evidence: Round 40 maker asks whether the Archive flow is complete; client requests a separate way to “genuinely get rid of a bookmark for good” and explicitly distinguishes “set aside” from “delete.”
decisions.note: At the archive specification gate, the client extends the scope with permanent deletion and its required distinction from Archive.

decisions.evidence: Round 41 maker presents “Delete permanently” followed by an irreversible confirmation; client confirms the bookmark disappears only after deliberate confirmation.
decisions.note: The revised flow supports permanent bookmark deletion.

decisions.evidence: Round 41 maker presents “Move to Archive” and “Delete permanently” as visibly separate actions; client says archiving feels reversible while deleting feels final and the two “never blur together.”
decisions.note: The decision clearly distinguishes reversible archive from permanent removal.

decisions.evidence: Round 45 maker presents rejecting `not a link`, leaving it unsaved, refocusing the field, and showing a valid-address example; client agrees that a bookmark requires “an actual address.”
decisions.note: The invalid-input behavior enforces the required URL constraint.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 46–47 present treating recognized tracking parameters and fragments as duplicate noise while preserving query data that selects different content; client explicitly confirms returning to the existing bookmark.
decisions.note: This duplicate-normalization edge case remains consistent with converging duplicate saves on the existing item.

decisions.evidence: Round 49 maker presents ` DESIGN ` being recognized as an already attached `design` tag rather than creating another; client confirms this prevents capitalization- and whitespace-based near-duplicates.
decisions.note: The edge behavior reinforces reuse of existing tags rather than creating duplicate tag identities.

decisions.evidence: Round 50 maker presents an unmatched opening quote retaining partial matches while prompting the user to close it; client confirms this is clearer than misleading exact results or an error.
decisions.note: The incomplete-input edge case is compatible with the established exact-phrase behavior.

decisions.evidence: Round 51 maker presents cancelling permanent deletion with “Keep bookmark,” returning to an unchanged card; client confirms nothing is removed or changed.
decisions.note: Cancellation preserves the bookmark and reinforces the deliberate distinction between retaining and permanently deleting it.

decisions.evidence: Round 52 maker asks whether Read Later and Archive states persist indefinitely until explicit user action; client confirms nothing should “move, expire, or disappear on its own.”
decisions.note: Persistent status until explicit read, restore, or delete action is consistent with the reference state model.

decisions.evidence: Round 53 maker presents compact truncation of unusually long titles, descriptions, and labels with “Show full details” on demand; client confirms it preserves everyday skimming while retaining access to full content.
decisions.note: This is a readability-first presentation choice that still exposes the bookmark details and is functionally consistent with the reference.
